"Canned" has a few related meanings, all connected by a single core idea: something that was made in advance, stored, and is ready to be used at any time — rather than being freshly made right now.
Meaning 1: Food preserved in a sealed metal container

The most literal meaning. Canned food has been cooked, sealed inside a metal tin, and can be stored for months or years without going bad.

canned tomatoes, canned tuna, canned soup, canned corn

This is the straightforward, physical sense of the word — you've certainly seen canned goods in a store.
Meaning 2: Pre-made, pre-recorded, or standardized (the more important meaning)

This is where "canned" gets interesting and widely used. It describes something that was prepared in advance, stored like a can of food, and is now being pulled out and used repeatedly — rather than being created fresh, in the moment, for this specific situation.

The key ideas this meaning carries:

It's not original. It was made once and is reused many times, often with little or no adjustment.

It lacks authenticity. Because it wasn't created specifically for this moment or this person, it can feel hollow, impersonal, or mechanical.

It's convenient but not genuine. Like canned soup — quick and easy, but not as good as something freshly made.

The classic example: canned laughter

Have you ever watched an old TV sitcom and heard a laughing sound every time a joke was made? That's canned laughter — pre-recorded laughing sounds that were added to the show in editing. No one is actually laughing in the moment at your TV. The producers recorded laughter once, stored it, and inserted it into the show wherever they wanted. It sounds artificial precisely because it is.

Canned response / canned reply

If you contact a company's customer service and receive a reply that feels like it was written for everyone and not specifically for you — it probably was. That's a canned response: a template answer, pre-written, stored, and sent out automatically or copy-pasted whenever a similar question comes in. It solves the problem quickly but feels impersonal.

Canned speech / canned presentation

A politician who travels city to city delivering essentially the same speech to every audience is giving a canned speech. A salesperson who walks into every meeting and delivers the same pitch word-for-word is giving a canned presentation. There's nothing spontaneous or tailored about it.

Canned answer

If someone asks you a difficult question and you immediately launch into a smooth, well-rehearsed explanation without thinking — you gave a canned answer. You had it prepared and waiting. (This can be neutral or even positive — being prepared isn't always a bad thing — but it often implies the answer felt a little too polished, a little too ready.)
The tone and feeling of the word

"Canned" in this figurative sense is usually mildly negative or dismissive. When someone calls something "canned," they're typically criticizing it for lacking:

  • Spontaneity — it wasn't created in the moment
  • Sincerity — it doesn't feel like it came from a real, thoughtful place
  • Originality — it's the same thing being reused again and again
  • Personal relevance — it wasn't made for you specifically

Saying "that was a canned response" is essentially saying: "They didn't actually think about my situation. They just pulled out a ready-made reply."

However, in some contexts "canned" is used neutrally, especially in professional settings. "I have a canned answer for this question" simply means "I've answered this so many times that I have a well-prepared reply" — without necessarily implying anything dishonest or lazy.
Meaning 3: Fired from a job (informal slang)

In informal American English, "canned" can mean dismissed from employment — fired. Just as a factory seals something in a can and sends it away, a company "cans" an employee and sends them away.

"He got canned after missing three deadlines."
"She was canned without any warning."

This usage is casual and a bit dated, but you'll still encounter it, especially in American films, novels, and informal speech.

In very informal, mostly older British and American slang, "canned" can mean intoxicated.

"He showed up to the party completely canned."

This meaning is uncommon today — you're unlikely to hear it much in modern everyday speech — but it appears in older literature and films.

Most common and important → Pre-made, pre-recorded, lacking originality or spontaneity (canned laughter, canned response, canned speech)

Literal/everyday → Food preserved in a metal tin (canned beans, canned fruit)

Informal → Fired from a job (got canned)

Rare/dated slang → Drunk (completely canned)

All meanings of "canned" trace back to the same image: a can is something sealed, preserved, and stored — ready for later use, but no longer fresh. Whether it's food, laughter, or a speech, calling something "canned" means it's been packaged in advance and stored for reuse, rather than being made fresh for the moment at hand.
